[PATH:empirical] Natural experiments from minimum wage hikes in cities like Seattle, San Francisco, or London, using administrative firm-level data on automation adoption (e.g., robot imports, software investment) and labor market tightness measures (e.g., vacancy rates, quits). — Directly tests the causal effect of large wage increases on automation in tight labor markets, leveraging quasi-experimental variation across cities and over time.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level surveys or case studies in high-productivity urban sectors (e.g., fast food, retail, logistics) that track investment decisions before and after a significant minimum wage increase, with controls for labor supply tightness. — Provides micro-level evidence on the mechanism—whether firms substitute capital for labor when wage costs rise and labor is scarce—complementing aggregate data.

[PATH:theoretical] Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018) or similar models of directed technical change, extended to incorporate minimum wage shocks and labor market frictions, calibrated to high-productivity urban markets. — Offers a formal framework to predict conditions under which automation accelerates, helping to isolate the effect of wage policy from other confounding factors.

qualifier.geographic: high-productivity urban markets in developed economies

[PATH:theoretical] Labor market equilibrium models incorporating human capital investment and wage floors (e.g., Acemoglu & Pischke 1999 framework) — Models predict whether firms substitute wage costs with training investment under productivity and turnover constraints; can clarify conditions under which the hypothesis holds.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on minimum wage impacts on firm-side training (e.g., from journals like Industrial and Labor Relations Review or Journal of Labor Economics) — Synthesizes prior empirical findings across urban markets, revealing consistent patterns or null results that can validate the disputed hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Panel data on firm-level training expenditures from high-productivity urban markets (e.g., U.S. metropolitan areas) during post-2000 minimum wage increases, matched with capital investment data from the U.S. Census Bureau's Annual Survey of Manufactures or Compustat. — Directly tests whether large minimum wage hikes in tight labor markets reduce per-worker training spending and increase capital substitution, using variation across time and geography.

[PATH:literature] Quasi-experimental studies exploiting state-level minimum wage changes (e.g., Card & Krueger 1994 replication with modern data) that analyze training outcomes and capital-labor ratios, particularly in retail and hospitality sectors where labor supply is abundant. — Leverages existing causal evidence to see if prior findings support or contradict the hypothesized capital-training trade-off under abundant labor conditions.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model with heterogeneous firms, endogenous training, and capital-labor substitution, calibrated to high-productivity urban economies. — Allows simulation of large wage shocks under varying labor supply elasticities to isolate the mechanism and test whether capital substitution dominates training investment when margins are squeezed.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level panel data from developed economies (e.g., U.S. Census Bureau's Annual Survey of Manufactures or Compustat) linking wage changes to training budgets and outsourcing contracts — Allows testing of the hypothesis by observing correlations between labor cost increases and shifts in training expenditure, controlling for industry and market productivity.

C011.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets
C011.object: a net decrease in within-firm wage inequality, as firms offset the wage floor by boosting performance-based pay for high-wage workers while freezing or reducing base pay for mid-wage workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets a net decrease in within-firm wage inequality, as firms offset the wage floor by boosting performance-based pay for high-wage workers while freezing or reducing base pay for mid-wage workers]

[PATH:empirical] Administrative payroll data from large retail and food-service firms in high-productivity urban markets (e.g., San Francisco, Seattle) before and after moderate minimum wage increases, tracking base pay, performance bonuses, and wage percentile distributions within firms over a two-year horizon. — Directly tests the hypothesized offset mechanism: whether firms raise performance-based pay for top earners while compressing or freezing mid-wage base pay, and whether this yields a net decrease in within-firm wage inequality.

[PATH:theoretical] Firm-level wage-setting models incorporating minimum wage floors and endogenous performance pay (e.g., efficiency wage or tournament theory frameworks), calibrated to high-productivity urban labor markets. — Evaluates the logical consistency and parameter sensitivity of the proposed causal chain, identifying conditions under which the net inequality decrease would or would not occur.

[PATH:literature] Existing quasi-experimental literature on minimum wage effects on wage dispersion, particularly studies using firm-level data (e.g., Cengiz et al. 2019; Dube, Lester, and Reich 2010) re-analyzed with a focus on within-firm inequality and performance-pay components. — Provides a benchmark of empirical findings in similar contexts and can be meta-analyzed to assess whether the hypothesized pattern has been observed or contradicted in prior work.

qualifier.temporal: over a two-year adjustment period following a moderate minimum wage increase
